implementation_notes: Model the buffered state as an immutable snapshot referenced by an `AtomicReference`: the writer builds the next frame privately and calls `getAndSet(finished)`, which 'atomically sets the value to newValue and returns the old value' with VarHandle memory effects, then retires the returned buffer; readers call `get()` (volatile semantics) and never lock. `lazySet`/`setRelease` is the cheaper release-store publication when a single writer is guaranteed and readers only need the acquire side. The swap is one reference exchange, so buffer size is irrelevant.
pitfalls: `lazySet`/`setPlain` relax ordering deliberately: use them only for an immutable snapshot with a single writer, never for a mutable buffer.
Publishing a snapshot and then mutating it (a reused mutable `ArrayList` as the frame) tears exactly as without the pattern.
Ignore the reference `getAndSet` returns and buffers leak; recycle it immediately and a slow reader may still be using it.
The field must be `final` and never reassigned - assigning a new AtomicReference defeats the publication guarantee.

variants.name: volatile field + full-snapshot write (single writer)
variants.idiom_name: private volatile Frame current with one publishing thread
variants.implementation_notes: With exactly one publishing thread, a `private volatile Frame current` field is the cheapest realization: the JLS gives volatile reads and writes the visibility and ordering needed for a reader to see either the previous or the new complete snapshot, and readers pay no CAS. The writer builds the next frame and assigns it; nothing else writes the field. As soon as more than one thread can publish, use the `AtomicReference` variant - two threads assigning a volatile field silently lose frames.
pitfalls: A volatile field is not mutual exclusion: concurrent writers still lose updates, and read-modify-write of the field is not atomic.
Volatile orders the reference, not the object graph: everything reachable from the frame must be safely published (final fields or effectively immutable).
Rebuilding the whole frame per publish allocates; only reuse buffers once the last reader of the previous snapshot has dropped it.

variants.name: AWT BufferStrategy (flip/blt rendering)
variants.implementation_notes: For rendering on a `Canvas` or `Window`, the JDK provides the double buffer: `getDrawGraphics()` 'creates a graphics context for the drawing buffer' (the back buffer), `show()` makes the drawing buffer visible (flip strategies are hardware-accelerated, blt strategies copy), and `contentsLost()`/`contentsRestored()` report that the platform invalidated or restored the buffer, so the frame must be redrawn. The documented `do { ... } while (contentsRestored()); show(); while (contentsLost())` loop is the canonical usage. Modern code should prefer JavaFX/Canvas or a GPU path, which composites offscreen.
pitfalls: Skipping the `contentsLost`/`contentsRestored` loops produces black or half-drawn frames after a resize or display change.
You must `dispose()` the Graphics obtained from `getDrawGraphics()` every iteration; leaking it leaks the back buffer.
`BufferStrategy` is per Canvas/Window - creating one per frame, or for an invisible component, throws or silently falls back to blt.
